lead: The unit explains how an AC mains supply becomes a steady DC rail: rectification, filtering, regulation and efficient conversion. You learn to choose a rectifier and filter, design a Zener or transistor regulator, read IC regulator data, and compare linear and switched supplies. After it you can calculate ripple, regulation, dissipation and duty cycle for small power-supply designs.
about: This unit starts with the diode as a one-way valve and builds a complete DC power supply. Chapter 1.1 compares half-wave, centre-tapped full-wave and bridge rectifiers. Chapter 1.2 adds capacitor and LC filters and defines ripple factor. Chapter 1.3 uses the same diode switch in clippers and clampers. Chapter 1.4 makes the Zener diode a shunt regulator, and Chapter 1.5 replaces it with series and shunt transistor regulators. Chapter 1.6 moves to IC regulators: 78xx, 79xx, LM317 and LDO. Chapter 1.7 explains switched-mode supplies and why they are efficient. Chapter 1.8, advanced, stacks diodes and capacitors into voltage multipliers. The order follows the signal: AC, rectified pulses, filtered DC, regulated DC, then efficient conversion.

chapters.idea: A rectifier converts AC into pulsating DC by allowing current through in one direction only.
chapters.depth: Compare half-wave, centre-tapped full-wave and bridge rectifiers. Derive Vdc, Irms, ripple frequency, PIV, transformer utilisation and efficiency for each. Some syllabi call the bridge the Graetz rectifier. Use ideal and practical diode drops; show waveforms for 230 V, 50 Hz mains step-down. Keep diode physics brief.

figure.title: Rectifier chain
figure.aria: Block diagram from AC mains through transformer, rectifier, filter and load; the rectifier block is highlighted.

chapters.example: A 230 V, 50 Hz mains is stepped down by a 10:1 transformer and fed to a half-wave rectifier with a 1 kΩ load and a silicon diode (Vd = 0.7 V). Find the peak load voltage, DC load voltage, ripple frequency and PIV of the diode.
chapters.trap: Using rms instead of peak in Vdc = Vm/π; forgetting the diode drop; bridge PIV is Vm, not 2Vm.
chapters.prereq: PN junction diode V-I, ideal-diode model, transformer rms and peak values.
chapters.leave: Diode capacitance and Schottky/tunnel diodes to earlier diode basics; precision rectifiers to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A filter reduces the AC ripple in rectified DC by storing energy or blocking alternating current.
chapters.depth: Capacitor-input filter: charging, discharge through load, ripple voltage and ripple factor for half-wave and full-wave. Use the approximate formulas Vr ≈ Vdc/(2fCR) for full-wave and Vr ≈ Vdc/(fCR) for half-wave. Cover RC and RLC passive filters, cut-off and attenuation. Some syllabi call these passive filters. Keep active filters to Unit 7.

figure.title: Capacitor filter action
figure.aria: Block diagram of a capacitor and LC filter: pulsating DC charges a capacitor, the capacitor discharges through the load, and an LC section gives smooth DC.

chapters.example: A full-wave bridge rectifier with Vm = 12 V, f = 50 Hz feeds a capacitor C = 1000 µF and load R = 100 Ω. Use the approximate capacitor-filter formulas. Find the ripple voltage, DC output and ripple factor.
chapters.trap: Using f instead of 2f for full-wave ripple; applying the capacitor formula when load current is too high; ignoring diode drop.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 rectifier waveforms; RC time constant and impedance.
chapters.leave: Active RC filters and Sallen-Key circuits to Unit 7; three-phase rectifiers are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: A clipper cuts off part of a waveform; a clamper shifts the whole waveform up or down in DC level.
chapters.depth: Series and shunt clippers with and without bias; positive, negative, biased and double clippers. Clampers: positive and negative, with ideal and practical diodes; effect of R and C time constant. Some syllabi call clippers limiting circuits. Use transfer characteristics and waveform sketches.

figure.aria: Plot of a 10 V sine input and its output clipped at +4 V; the output is flat at +4 V on positive peaks.

chapters.example: A 10 V peak, 50 Hz sine wave drives a shunt positive clipper with an ideal diode in series with a 4 V battery. The diode conducts when the input exceeds 4 V. Sketch input and output for one cycle and state the output peak-to-peak.
chapters.trap: Reversing diode or battery changes the clip level; a clamper changes DC average but not peak-to-peak; the capacitor may charge to the wrong polarity.
chapters.prereq: Diode switch model, RC time constant, sine wave peak and average.
chapters.leave: Precision clipping with op-amps to Unit 6; waveform generators to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A reverse-biased Zener diode maintains an almost constant voltage and shunts excess current to regulate a load.
chapters.depth: Zener V-I characteristic, breakdown, Iz(min), Iz(max), power rating. Design Rs for line and load variation. Load regulation and line regulation. Some syllabi call it a Zener shunt regulator. Include numerical design and power derating.

figure.title: Zener shunt regulator
figure.aria: Block diagram of a Zener shunt regulator: 12 V input through 220 Ω to a 6 V Zener and 1 kΩ load; the Zener carries 21.3 mA.

chapters.example: A Zener regulator has Vin = 12 V, Vz = 6 V, Rs = 220 Ω and RL = 1 kΩ. Find the Zener current and power. Then find the minimum RL that keeps Iz ≥ 5 mA.
chapters.trap: Assuming regulation when Iz is below the knee; ignoring Zener power; Rs too large gives poor regulation, too small burns the Zener.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 filtered DC; Zener reverse characteristic.
chapters.leave: Precision voltage references and temperature-compensated Zeners to advanced study; transistor regulators to Chapter 1.5.

chapters.idea: A transistor regulator compares a sample of the output with a reference and controls a pass or shunt device to hold the output steady.
chapters.depth: Series pass regulator with error amplifier, reference and feedback divider; shunt regulator; current limiting and thermal shutdown in outline. Derive Vout = Vref(1 + R1/R2). Compare efficiency and dissipation. Some syllabi call these discrete regulators. Keep op-amp internal design to Unit 5.

figure.title: Series regulator
figure.aria: Series regulator block diagram: 5.6 V reference and error amplifier drive a pass transistor to 8.4 V; a 10 kΩ and 20 kΩ divider feeds back to the error amplifier.

chapters.example: A series regulator uses Vref = 5.6 V, R1 = 10 kΩ from Vout to the error amplifier and R2 = 20 kΩ from the error amplifier to ground. Vin = 12 V and load current is 84 mA. Find Vout and the pass-transistor power dissipation.
chapters.trap: Swapping R1 and R2 in the feedback formula; using Vout instead of Vin−Vout for pass-transistor dissipation; forgetting dropout voltage.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 Zener reference; BJT biasing and small-signal models from Unit 2.
chapters.leave: Op-amp error amplifier design to Unit 5; feedback stability to Unit 4; IC regulator internals to Chapter 1.6.

chapters.idea: An IC regulator integrates a reference, error amplifier and pass transistor to give a fixed or adjustable output in a small package.
chapters.depth: 78xx positive fixed, 79xx negative fixed, LM317 adjustable, LDO low-dropout. Pinout, input/output capacitors, dropout, quiescent current, thermal calculation, PSRR and stability in outline. Some syllabi call them three-terminal regulators. Keep detailed PSRR and bandwidth to Unit 4/5.

figure.aria: Tree of IC regulator families: 78xx fixed positive, 79xx fixed negative, LM317 adjustable and LDO low dropout.

chapters.example: A 7805 gives 5 V from Vin = 12 V at Iload = 500 mA. Find its power dissipation and the heatsink thermal resistance needed if ambient is 40 °C and junction maximum is 125 °C. The junction-to-case thermal resistance is 5 °C/W and case-to-heatsink is 1 °C/W.
chapters.trap: LM317 keeps 1.25 V between OUT and ADJ, not to ground; 79xx is negative; dropout is not the same as quiescent current.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.5 discrete regulator; feedback from Unit 4; thermal resistance basics.
chapters.leave: Detailed PSRR, bandwidth and stability to Unit 4/5; switching converter control to Chapter 1.7.

chapters.idea: A switched-mode supply chops input power at high frequency and uses inductors or capacitors to transfer energy, regulating output by duty cycle.
chapters.depth: Buck, boost and buck-boost in outline; duty-cycle formulas in continuous conduction; switching loss, ripple, diode versus synchronous rectification; why efficiency is high. Some syllabi call these switching regulators. Keep control-loop compensation brief.

figure.title: Buck converter idea
figure.aria: Buck converter block diagram: 24 V input switched at duty 0.4, through 100 µH energy storage and an output filter to 9.6 V; PWM feedback controls the switch.

chapters.example: A buck converter has Vin = 24 V, duty cycle D = 0.4, switching frequency fsw = 100 kHz and inductor L = 100 µH. Find the ideal output voltage and the inductor current ripple in continuous conduction.
chapters.trap: Swapping buck and boost duty formulas; buck Vout = D Vin, boost Vout = Vin/(1−D); ignoring diode drop and switching losses.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.6 linear regulators; inductor and capacitor energy storage.
chapters.leave: Control-loop compensation and EMI to advanced power electronics; op-amp comparators to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Voltage multipliers use diodes and capacitors to add peak voltages, producing DC at multiples of the input peak.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Half-wave and full-wave doublers, cascade tripler and quadrupler; no-load output, diode drops, ripple and load regulation. Keep it short: charge-pump action and one design example.

figure.title: Multiplier ladder
figure.aria: Diode-capacitor ladder for a voltage multiplier: a 10 V peak input is clamped and pumped through four stages to no-load outputs of 20 V, 30 V or 40 V.

chapters.example: A cascade voltage multiplier is driven by a 10 V peak, 50 Hz source with ideal diodes and capacitors. Find the no-load DC output for a doubler, a tripler and a quadrupler. Then repeat the doubler with diodes having Vd = 0.7 V.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that each stage adds a diode drop under load; expecting a multiplier to hold voltage at high load current; using rms instead of peak input.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 rectifier and Chapter 1.2 capacitor filter; diode switch model.
chapters.leave: Charge-pump IC design and high-voltage multipliers to advanced power electronics; regulation to Chapters 1.4–1.7.
